name: Johns Hopkins Center for Health Security (charityevals)
beneficiaries_note: Our build: a pandemic kills people everywhere and the future lost is everyone's, so the result is spread by world population.
summary: The Johns Hopkins Center for Health Security (Baltimore), part of Johns Hopkins University, works to prevent and prepare for pandemics: biosecurity policy research and advocacy, outbreak analytics for CDC and health departments (CORI) and training. Gifts go through the university's form for the Center; it publishes no accounts, so this model of all its work in 2025 builds its budget (about $13.8M) from its published grants. At the defaults it averts about {{result}} years of healthy life per $1,000, from {{low}} to {{high}} on its plausible range: each dollar is valued as a typical project's cut in the forecast risk of pandemics (Rethink Priorities' cross-cause model, the Existential Risk Persuasion Tournament's experts), deaths valued like every death (a COVID-scale pandemic's at COVID's age mix) and the future lost counted through the discount rate. The biggest uncertainty is how much a dollar of such work cuts the risk (Rethink calls its figures placeholders; the range runs ten times either way); the result also moves with the discount rate and the years a cut counts. Every branch is discounted for missing data: no outcome of the work on the risk is measured.

sections.title: Other outcomes, in this model's unit
sections.explainer: charityevals' standard step for outcomes in more than one unit (docs/normalization.md 2.6): each outcome is counted in its own unit (units of value for income and deaths, WELLBYs for life satisfaction, tonnes of CO₂e, chicken pain days) and put into this model's unit by its unit's conversion over this unit's, which the headline's conversion cancels. So each moves only with its own sliders, exactly as in a model of its own unit. The rows are fixed; don't edit them.

rows.label: Share of the Center's budget those published grants make up
rows.explainer: The rest comes from funders who publish no amounts: other federal agencies (NSF, DTRA), WHO, foundations (the Nuclear Threat Initiative and Founders Pledge members are listed among its funders), individual donors and the university. Anchor: in 2017 Open Philanthropy's grant ($5.3M a year) took the Center's budget from $5.3M to about $8M (Open Philanthropy's grant page), two thirds of it; business-database estimates put its 2025 revenue near $10M (the high end). Our judgment, 70% (45% to 95%).

rows.label: The Center's spending in 2025 (all its work)
rows.explainer: The Center's yearly money, built from its published grants over the share of its budget they are (Convention 1: no accounts or budget of its own are published). Every programme is modelled: biosecurity and pandemic policy research (AI and biosecurity, DNA synthesis screening, tabletop exercises), outbreak analytics for CDC and health departments (CORI), the journal Health Security, and training (the Emerging Leaders in Biosecurity fellowship, doctoral scholarships). A donor gives through Johns Hopkins University's gift form for the Center (secure.jhu.edu/form/CHS); the budget is the Center's own. The grants include the university's indirect costs, so nothing is added for overhead.

rows.label: How far a typical project's effect applies to the Center's biosecurity policy work
rows.explainer: The Center's research is taken up more than a typical project's: it framed global catastrophic biological risks (its 2017 working definition), its pandemic exercises (Clade X, Event 201) are used by governments, it is a WHO and PAHO Collaborating Centre, and its scholars testify to Congress (Jassi Pannu on gene synthesis and AI-designed agents, December 2025). Much of its research is on ordinary public-health preparedness, with a longer path to a catastrophe. Net 0.9, our judgment, 0.4 to 1.3.

rows.label: How far a typical project's effect applies to CORI's outbreak analytics
rows.explainer: CORI builds risk assessments (measles, mpox), forecasting tools and a network of health departments testing outbreak response (ORI-Net): faster response helps in a COVID-scale pandemic too, but the work is aimed at ordinary outbreaks, so its path to the pandemic risks counted is thinner than a typical biosecurity project's. Our judgment, 0.4 (0.1 to 0.8); the good it does in ordinary outbreaks is in unmodelled_benefits_adj.

rows.label: Healthy years per unit of value of the deaths averted (for the weights below)
rows.explainer: The bridge's healthy years over the deaths' value: turns each branch's deaths into healthy years for the weights.

rows.label: Weight: healthy years from the pandemic work (policy research and CORI) (before adjustments)
rows.formula: bio_deaths_averted * ((1 - bio_covid_scale_share) * value_per_death + bio_covid_scale_share * covid_value_per_death) * dalys_per_death_value + bio_future_dalys
rows.explainer: The branch's deaths averted in healthy years (its COVID-scale part at COVID-19's age mix), plus its future healthy years kept: its share of the value, used to weight the adjustments so each applies to its own branch's value.

rows.label: Weight: healthy years from the training (before adjustments)
rows.formula: fb_deaths_averted * ((1 - bio_covid_scale_share) * value_per_death + bio_covid_scale_share * covid_value_per_death) * dalys_per_death_value + fb_future_dalys
rows.explainer: The branch's deaths averted in healthy years (its COVID-scale part at COVID-19's age mix), plus its future healthy years kept: its share of the value, used to weight the adjustments so each applies to its own branch's value.

rows.label: Pandemic work: how far a typical project's effect applies (CORI and the policy work)
rows.explainer: CORI's and the policy work's multipliers, weighted by their spending within the pandemic branch (Convention 7): within the branch a dollar of each counts the same before adjustments.

rows.label: How far the typical project's effect applies to this charity's work
rows.explainer: Branch by branch: the pandemic work at bio_evidence_adj (CORI's and the policy work's multipliers by their budgets), the training at the policy work's multiplier. Weighted by each branch's healthy years (w_bio, w_fb), so each multiplier applies to its own branch's value.

rows.label: Share of the work no one else would have done now
rows.explainer: The share of the work no one else would have done now: other groups do biosecurity policy (NTI | bio, Georgetown's Center for Global Health Science and Security, RAND, the Council on Strategic Risks) and CDC funds other outbreak-analytics centres in its Insight Net, but the Center is the oldest and largest US academic biosecurity centre. Our judgment, 0.7 (0.4 to 0.9); that the work would have come years later is in years_of_impact.

rows.label: This charity's share of the resources behind the outcome
rows.explainer: The Center's share of the resources behind its outputs: CORI works under a cooperative agreement with CDC's Center for Forecasting and Outbreak Analytics (CDC's own staff time) and with health departments; exercises and meetings bring partners' staff time; the rest is the Center's own. Our judgment, 0.85 (0.6 to 1).

rows.label: This charity's share of the good done with money, work or budgets it brings in
rows.explainer: The site's one setting for resources another party commits only because of the organisation (docs/normalization.md 2.24): governments' budgets and enforcement, companies' compliance, the use others make of research. The charity is credited this share of the good done with them, net of their cost; the rest stays with those who paid or did the work. Fixed.

rows.label: Share of credit used
rows.explainer: The share among co-advocates times the mobiliser's share: the rest of the credit stays with those who carry out the result (docs/normalization.md 2.24).

rows.label: Leverage and funging
rows.explainer: Coefficient Giving, the Center's main unrestricted funder, may give less if small donors give more, and a gift through Johns Hopkins could free university money for other uses; no sign of either is published (its smaller 2023 renewal is read as money getting scarcer, in the next-dollar figure). 0.9 (0.7 to 1.05), our judgment.

rows.label: Counted less where the outcome isn't measured for this charity
rows.explainer: Thin: no outcome of the Center's work on the risk is measured; the cut per dollar is a typical project's from Rethink Priorities' model and the chances are forecasts, so the shared missing-data step applies (docs/normalization.md 2.12).

rows.label: All adjustments combined
rows.explainer: The product of the adjustments above.

rows.label: Benefits not modelled, as a share of modelled value
rows.explainer: Good beyond the pandemics counted: CORI's analytics and the Center's preparedness research help health departments in ordinary outbreaks (measles, mpox, H5N1), far smaller than COVID-scale and outside the chain, and the journal Health Security serves the field. No outbreak deaths averted are measured. Anchor: at 5% this is about 2 years of healthy life per $1,000 of CORI's spending, in the range of the site's rich-country services and research models (cancer research and refugee services about 2, the American Red Cross about 4.5); 0 to 20% (up to about 7.5), our judgment.

rows.label: Harm: speeding up dangerous capabilities, as a share of modelled value
rows.explainer: A typical project's chance of backfiring is already in the shared cut per dollar (Rethink Priorities' backfire step). The Center builds no capabilities: its AI and biosecurity work argues for oversight of biological AI models and synthesis screening. 0, down to −3% for analyses that also map what AI can do. Our judgment.

rows.label: Harm: information hazards and attention, as a share of modelled value
rows.explainer: Beyond a typical project's backfire: its pandemic exercises became a focus of conspiracy theories (Event 201, a coronavirus scenario run in October 2019, was cited as proof the COVID-19 pandemic was planned, and the Center put out statements against that), which may have cost the response some trust; published analyses of pathogens' characteristics can point to a weapon. −2%, from −8% to 0, our judgment.
